$comment: The principals the RULES and /api/orgs/datasets must answer identically
about, in one table so neither suite can drift into asserting its own
expectations.
cloud/rules-org-data-permission.spec.mjs seeds these into the emulator
and asks Firestore. apps/console/specs/dataset-write-authority-agrees
.spec.ts runs the server's own resolver over the same rows. Both sides
ask "Manage data" (`data.manage`) and nothing about the role (AGL-4047):
its default is the owner, admin and editor, a custom role or a per-member
override decides it for ANY role, and dataset UPDATES and record
update/deletes go client-direct, gated by the rules alone. The first
defect this table pinned ran the other way: the rules read the raw `role`
while the API resolved a custom role, so an editor whose `data.manage` was
revoked was refused by the API and permitted by the rules.
`member` is the document AS STORED. A row with no `resolvedPermissions`
key is a member whose document predates the field or was written by a
path that bypasses the projection; those rows are the point, not an
oversight.
`customRole` is what `orgs/{orgId}/roles/{roleId}` holds. The rules never
read it — that is the whole reason the resolved map is denormalized — but
the API does, so the agreement assertion needs it.
`mayWriteDatasets` is the ONE expected verdict. `rulesOnly` rows are
excluded from the agreement check because the API expresses that
condition through a different mechanism (suspension is `lockdownRefusal`
there, not a permission).
The seeded dataset is shared with the workspace and with `host:host-a`, so
the site collaborator rows reach it and a refusal of theirs is about the
key, not the scope.

principals.note: The baseline. If this is ever false the ruleset locks out every workspace.
A plain editor: `data.manage` is an editor default.
A viewer holds nothing by default. Refused on both sides.
An admin with no resolved map: the key's default for the role, which for an admin is yes.

A site collaborator with Author access to host-a (a workspace viewer scoped to one site), granted nothing. They reach the dataset and hold no `data.manage` by default: refused on the key, not the scope.
THE DEFECT. An editor whose custom role revokes `data.manage`. The API refused this principal; the rules, reading only `role`, permitted every dataset and record write they already had.
A custom role GRANTING `data.manage` to a viewer. Permitted by both (AGL-4047): the key decides and a role is only its preset. Before, a role gate led on both sides and refused this principal.
Three layers, in order: the custom role revokes and the per-member override puts it back. The precedence the rules could not have reimplemented, arriving pre-resolved.

NO resolvedPermissions AT ALL — the shape of every member written before the field existed. Must resolve to the key's default for the role, which for an editor is yes. If this is false the deploy is a mass lockout.
The same absent map on a VIEWER. The control that stops 'absent' reading as 'everything allowed': an absent key reads as the role's default, and a viewer's default is no.

No resolved map, but a per-member override that revokes. The middle rung of the default chain — without it an unprojected member silently regains a permission the console and the API both refuse them.
An editor whose OWN permissions deny `data.manage`, as the projection stamps it: the per-member layer refuses the role's default.
A viewer whose OWN permissions grant `data.manage`, as the projection stamps it (AGL-4047): the key decides.
A viewer granted `data.manage` by a per-member override the projection has not stamped yet. The rules read the override where no resolved map exists, as the API resolves it.
A resolved map that says nothing about `data.manage`. The rule must read the KEY, not the presence of the field.
Every permission granted and the org suspended. The suspension conjunct still leads, so a permission map cannot buy a write back.
